newsitem.title: USA: Gore should weather fund-raising storm -- analysts.
newsitem.headline: Gore should weather fund-raising storm -- analysts.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, U.S. Political Correspondent

Vice President Al Gore may have tarnished his squeaky clean image by admitting he raised campaign funds from his White House office, but analysts say the affair should not seriously dent his presidential chances.
"This will be something of a millstone around his neck, but a millstone he will probably be able to bear," said David Birdsell, a political scientist at Baruch College in New York.

In a hastily called news conference at the White House on Monday designed to quell a growing uproar over his fund-raising activities, Gore acknowledged he made "a few" telephone calls from his White House office asking for donations to the Democratic Party.

He said the calls were charged to a DNC credit card so the expense was not paid by the federal government. Gore insisted he had received legal advice that he had not violated the Hatch Act, which bans political fund raising by government officials on federal property.

"I'm proud of what I did. I do not feel like I did anything wrong, much less illegal," Gore said. But he acknowledged public disquiet with the issue and said he would not be making "any such calls ever again."

Reaction from Republicans and newspaper editorial writers was largely negative. The New York Times said Gore's admission made imperative the appointment of an independent counsel to look into Democratic fund raising.

The Baltimore Sun said Gore, whose reputation for personal integrity had previously been largely unchallenged, had fallen victim to a common disease of anyone closely associated with President Bill Clinton.

"Suicide, indictment, prison, betrayal, derision, disgrace, defeat, dismissal -- there seems to be no end to the ravages of this illness. Now the latest victim, the Vice President, may be on the way to a rest home rather than the White House in 2000," the newspaper said.
But political analysts around the country said Gore remained the overwhelming front runner for the Democratic presidential nomination in 2000.

"I'd be surprised if there was any serious damage in the long run although he may have a problem if there are more revelations," said John Geer, a political scientist at Vanderbilt University in Nashville, Tennessee.

Gore has already moved decisively to create an aura of inevitability around his candidacy. He has placed supporters in key White House and Democratic Party positions around the country and has relentlessly wooed potential financial donors.
No other Democrat will be able to match his organisation, money or name recognition. But Gore remains dependent on Clinton and the fortunes of the administration.
Other Democrats who may run include House Minority Leader Dick Gephardt, former New Jersey Sen. Bill Bradley, Massachusetts Sen. John Kerry and Nebraska Sen. Bob Kerrey.
None have made any overt presidential steps, although all are no doubt observing Gore's troubles with considerable interest, biding their time in case he seriously stumbles.

"Gore's main challenge is to keep the other Democrats out of the race. This is not something voters outside of Washington DC care about very deeply," said Patrick Kinney, a political scientist at Arizona State University.

Polls show the scandal has yet to dent Clinton or Gore's popularity. Most voters seem to believe both parties skirt the campaign fund-raising rules and though many believe the president may have acted unethically, a majority believe he did not break the law.
"There's no criterion stating you have to be squeaky clean to be elected president. Look at Clinton," said Allan Lichtman of the American University in Washington.

The closest parallel to Gore may be George Bush, who as vice president was embroiled in the "Iran contra" affair, under which the Reagan administration sold arms to Iran to secure the release of U.S. hostages in Lebanon, and illegally sent the proceeds to right-wing rebels in Nicaragua.
The affair haunted and embarrassed Bush but did not stop him being elected president in 1988.
